<SUMMARY>Global geopolitical competition intensified this week across critical technology and resource sectors, particularly in semiconductors, AI, and rare earth minerals. The United States under President Donald Trump is accelerating efforts to onshore critical mineral processing and semiconductor development through significant investments and military base initiatives. Europe is actively pursuing its own AI infrastructure with substantial funding commitments, while simultaneously navigating American AI export control strategies. Maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz deteriorated following an attack on a Singapore-flagged cargo ship by Iran's IRGC, prompting a pause in international safe passage initiatives and raising oil price concerns. India remains a key partner in US discussions on AI model regulation and supply chain resilience, while also pursuing its own ambitious electronics manufacturing and energy security targets. China is expanding its manufacturing capabilities and hosting major supply chain expos focused on AI and green transition, underscoring its pivotal role in global supply networks.</SUMMARY>
<EWS>The attack on a Singapore-flagged cargo ship by Iran’s IRGC in the Strait of Hormuz, followed by the suspension of international safe passage programs and Iran’s warning regarding routes, indicates a heightened risk of maritime conflict and disruption to global energy and trade supply chains. The US Treasury’s sanctions on a network smuggling conflict minerals from Congo to Rwanda highlight persistent ethical sourcing challenges and potential disruptions in global tech supply. The significant increase in memory chip prices, described by Elon Musk as the largest he’s seen, suggests looming cost pressures for technology consumers and could impact future investments. Geopolitical risks associated with relying on foreign AI models, as raised in US-India talks, indicate a growing concern over AI supply chain dependencies and national security implications.</EWS>
<EXEC>
**Asia:**
MKS Inc. is expanding its Atotech equipment manufacturing site in Guangzhou, China, to enable the next wave of AI build-out. The Fourth China International Supply Chain Expo (CISCE) in Beijing opened its Healthy Life Chain section, drawing over 100 companies and debuting an AI zone, with participants highlighting green transition and AI as key drivers for supply chain efficiency. Washington needs allies to make AI export controls work, as expanding export controls are being considered to slow China’s AI progress. Kazakhstan secured agreements and MoUs valued at over $12 billion during President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to the EU, including the purchase of 50 Airbus passenger jets for €7.1 billion, aimed at expanding energy and trade ties.

**Europe:**
Judith Dada wrote about Europe needing an ambitious political agenda to respond to America’s AI warning shot. Italy and France are hesitant about a European Union proposal to ban former Russian combatants from entering the bloc. Europe is pushing back on Washington’s chip war.

**Americas:**
The US Army will allow several companies to build critical minerals processing plants at military bases around the country as part of President Donald Trump’s administration push for more domestic production. The US invested $250 million in I-Pulse for semiconductor and pulsed-power development under the CHIPS Act. Cirba Solutions testified before Congress to strengthen critical mineral supply chains and reduce reliance on China. The Grid Acceleration Coalition reaffirmed its call to speed up building critical transmission projects that drive economic growth and lower customer costs. Nokia announced a major expansion of its U.S. Semiconductor Advanced Test and Packaging in Pennsylvania to bolster AI growth.

**Oceania:**
Australia, Canada, and the UK issued a joint statement on energy and climate cooperation. The US proposed an AI partnership with the EU to secure semiconductor supply chains.</EXEC>
<LITHO>
**Asia:**
MKS Inc. announced the expansion of its Atotech equipment manufacturing site in Guangzhou, China, to support the next wave of AI build-out. OpenAI teamed with Broadcom to reveal Jalapeño, a custom AI chip built specifically for inference.

**Europe:**
IBM introduced a new transistor architecture at the 0.7nm (7-angstrom) node, called the industry’s first sub-1nm semiconductor technology, packing nearly 100 billion transistors. Applied Materials introduced new systems to accelerate DRAM and advanced packaging for AI chips. Europe is scaling 6-inch photonic chip production for mass manufacturing. The ASML China EUV saga points to a tougher reality for China’s chip sector.

**Americas:**
The US invested $250 million in I-Pulse for semiconductor and pulsed-power development, aiming to reduce reliance on foreign-chip supply chains. Nvidia’s Rubin will use 45°C direct-to-chip liquid cooling. Netris secured a $15 million Series A from a16z to automate AI data center networking. Dell Technologies introduced the PowerEdge XE8812, a new liquid-cooled server platform designed for large-scale inference and high-performance computing workloads, built around the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL4.

**Oceania:**
Cisco Secure Connect has planned maintenance for Meraki SD-WAN Head-End in Singapore and Australia from 2026-07-02 16:00 UTC to 2026-07-02 20:00 UTC.</LITHO>
<REE>
**Africa:**
The US Treasury sanctioned a network smuggling conflict minerals from Congo to Rwanda. Zimbabwe is scrutinizing Chinese lithium mining. Congo’s cobalt catalyst is shaping global markets amid a strategic shift.

**Americas:**
The US Army will allow several companies to build critical minerals processing plants at military bases. Cirba Solutions testified before Congress to strengthen critical mineral supply chains and reduce reliance on China. GoldHaven Resources Corp. completed a 2,320-line-kilometre airborne geophysical survey over its 100%-owned Magno Critical Minerals Project in British Columbia. Chile, a major global player in critical minerals like copper and lithium, presents a strategic alliance opportunity for India.

**Oceania:**
Australia, Canada, and the UK issued a joint statement on energy and climate cooperation. Visual Capitalist mapped which countries hold the biggest mineral reserves.</REE>
<GEO>
**Asia:**
The Fourth China International Supply Chain Expo (CISCE) opened its Healthy Life Chain section in Beijing, drawing over 100 leading companies. Kazakhstan secured agreements and MoUs valued at over $12 billion with the EU, including a key deal for the purchase of 50 Airbus passenger jets for €7.1 billion, to expand energy and trade ties.

**Europe:**
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to the EU’s headquarters in Brussels yielded agreements and MoUs potentially valued at over $12 billion. EU-Kazakhstan relations continue to have connectivity at their core. Sunwoda launched its next-generation 588Ah-Based ESS Platform at ees Europe 2026 in Munich, showcasing a broad portfolio of energy storage technologies.

**Americas:**
Deckorators opened its first Northeast manufacturing plant in Lackawanna, New York, adding 50 new jobs and doubling production capacity for its Surestone technology decking products.</GEO>
<MILITARY>
**Americas:**
The US Army opened military bases for critical minerals processing plants as part of a push for more domestic production, an initiative that could enhance national security.

**Europe:**
Italy and France are hesitant about a European Union proposal to ban former Russian combatants from entering the bloc.

**Oceania:**
Voronoi by Visual Capitalist ranked military spending growth by country in 2025. Foreign Policy published an article on restocking the Pentagon.</MILITARY>
<CONCLUSION>
**Americas:**
Apple’s stock plunged 5%, erasing $275 billion, following price hikes for its MacBook Pro, which now starts at $2,000, and iPads. Elon Musk called the memory chip price jump the biggest he has seen, highlighting a growing divide between thriving chipmakers and struggling tech consumers. Micron Technology’s Q3 earnings beat expectations, sending its stock surging 18% premarket and lifting chip stocks worldwide. Nasdaq futures surged 2% as chip outlook calmed AI jitters. Rystad Energy projects the fuel cell market to hit $30 billion by 2030, driven by AI data center demand.

**Africa:**
Lithium carbonate futures in China fell approximately 10% over two trading sessions, dropping to a 10-week low of about 157,000 yuan ($23,175) per tonne, following market speculation about a CATL supply surge.

**Europe:**
Solstice and TensorX announced a partnership to finance European sovereign AI infrastructure, committing up to $1 billion in capacity to finance AI hardware and data-center buildout.</CONCLUSION>
<INDIA>India's impending trade agreement with the US is centered on gaining a tariff advantage over competitors like China and Vietnam, with teams fine-tuning details. India highlighted its ambitious energy storage and nuclear targets at a BRICS meeting in New Delhi, where BRICS Energy Ministers stressed energy security and advocated for diversified, resilient, and transparent energy systems and supply chains. The US and India are holding crucial talks on releasing advanced AI models, including those from Anthropic, prioritizing a secure and gradual approach to ensure critical infrastructure safety; these high-stakes talks highlight geopolitical risks of relying on foreign AI models, potentially accelerating India's domestic AI development. An India-Chile partnership aims to integrate value chains for AI and data center inputs, leveraging Chile’s position as a major player in copper and lithium. India’s ambition to build a $500 billion electronics industry by 2030 presents a major opportunity for MSMEs, focusing on skills and innovation, while acknowledging it still trails China in manufacturing scale. Crisil Ratings' stress test indicated India Inc remains broadly resilient despite a prolonged West Asia conflict due to stronger balance sheets, steady domestic demand, and government support. The US announced PaxPass to streamline the movement of critical AI goods at the Pax Silica summit. The US and India aligned to cut AI supply chain risks under Pax Silica, explaining how India matters to the global AI supply chain pact. Skewed investment and distorted competition are weakening India’s growth engine, with capital deployed to protect margins rather than expand output.</INDIA>
<WEST_ASIA>President Donald Trump asked Congress for billions more for the Iran war, despite reports of a memorandum of understanding to end it. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attacked a Singapore-flagged cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz, asserting control over the waterway. The Hormuz evacuation was suspended following this attack in the Gulf of Oman, and the UN International Maritime Organization (IMO) paused its program to shepherd ships and seafarers through the Strait. Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority warned that ships using routes outside the designated framework "will not be covered by safe passage guarantees." NATO boss Rutte backed President Donald Trump’s Iran operation. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the US would not reach a deal with Iran at “any price” and rejected tolls in the Strait of Hormuz. Asian refiners reduced their spot purchases of Middle East crude for this month and next, following three weeks of increased buying, due to lingering uncertainties about the navigability of the Strait. The Iran war impacts Abu Dhabi's AI plans. Israel’s New AI Directorate is an opening for the U.S., as Israel has already operationalized AI integration. A US-Iran peace deal grants access to Tehran's nuclear sites, according to the UN watchdog. Oil prices extended gains on concern over potential US-Iran conflict. The Iran conflict has reshaped energy resilience.</WEST_ASIA>
<FINAL_CONCLUSION>The ongoing strategic competition for technological supremacy, particularly in AI and semiconductors, will continue to drive significant investment and policy actions, as evidenced by US CHIPS Act funding and European sovereign AI initiatives. The US will likely intensify efforts to secure critical mineral supply chains domestically and through alliances, potentially leading to further sanctions on conflict mineral networks. Maritime tensions in the Strait of Hormuz present a critical vulnerability for global energy markets and necessitate sustained diplomatic engagement and contingency planning to prevent escalation. India's growing role in global AI and electronics supply chains, coupled with its energy security ambitions, positions it as a crucial strategic partner for the US, driving ongoing high-stakes discussions on AI governance and trade. The divergence in approaches to AI export controls between the US and Europe indicates potential friction points that will require careful management to maintain allied cohesion.</FINAL_CONCLUSION>
